item.title: New Suicide Prevention Research
item.description:
Suicide

New Suicide Prevention Research

Research offers tools, strategies, and hope for at-risk individuals.

Posted September 30, 2026

Key points
  • Suicide affects people of all ages and backgrounds.
  • The 988 Suicide and Crisis Helpline has proven highly effective.
  • Promising new research initiatives offer new and innovative tools and strategies.

Suicide is a universally acknowledged global problem, and one that affects people across all age groups, social backgrounds, and economic circumstances. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), over 700 thousand people die by suicide each year, and suicide is the third leading cause of death in 15-29-year-olds and, overall, the 10th leading cause of death in the US.

Since 2008, when September was declared Suicide Prevention Awareness Month, organizations such as the International Organization for Suicide Prevention and The National Action Alliance for Suicide Prevention (Action Alliance) have devoted efforts and resources to ending the culture of silence, raising awareness around prevention and support, and guiding individuals who are struggling toward effective interventions and treatments, as well as those who are living with the long-term impacts of the suicide of a loved one.

A promising statistic amid persistent concerns

According to research published in The Lancet in 2025, while suicide remains an urgent and serious global health issue, there has been a decline (of 39.5%) in suicides globally since 1990. Despite this decline, suicide persists as “a leading cause of death of young people in many areas of the world.”

Hotlines prove a valuable resource for adolescents and young adults

New research reveals the positive impact of suicide prevention among adolescents and young people since the inception of the 988 Suicide and Crisis Helpline in 2022, with rates dropping “11 percent below projections,” and decreasing most strongly in states with “higher volumes of answered calls,” according to an April 2026 New York Times article.

Small joys and suicide prevention

Research led by Philip Resnik, a computational linguist in the Department of Linguistics and Institute for Advanced Computer Studies at the University of Maryland, was published in July of 2026 and examined over 16,648 self-reports of individuals who had struggled with suicidal thoughts and shared their reasons to live. Research cited several categories as suicide deterrents, including concern for loved ones and pets, appreciation of small pleasures like food, music, and leisure activities, and anticipation of, and awareness of, the possibility of conditions improving in the future.

Effective restrictions to means

A systematic review of suicide means restrictions, including jumping restrictions, restrictions on package sizing of medications, restrictions of access to pesticides and pesticide bans, and the detoxification of fuels, showed promising results.

Small sample sizes limited results on restricting access to firearms. However, research from Weill Cornell Medicine and UC Berkeley School of Public Health that examined data from Massachusetts, New Jersey, New Mexico, and Rhode Island cited positive outcomes of temporary firearms restrictions for individuals at high risk of self-harm.

Promising new predictive research on the horizon

Highly anticipated research, led by suicide-prevention researcher Matthew K. Nock, Edgar Pierce Professor of Psychology at Harvard University, slated for publication in October of 2026, will introduce a new and highly effective model that accurately predicts both suicidal crises and actual suicide attempts a week in advance.

If you or someone you know is in crisis
It is important to know that you are not alone … and it is important to seek help.

If you or someone you know is struggling with dark thoughts of having to escape or self-harm, there are emergency resources and mental health professionals standing by to help you.

Mental Health & Crisis Resources
If you or someone you know is in immediate danger or experiencing a medical emergency, call 911 or go to the nearest emergency department.

USA
988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline
Call or text: 988. Free, confidential crisis support is available 24 hours a day, 7 days a week.

Crisis Text Line
Text HOME to 741741. Free, 24/7 emotional support from a trained crisis counsellor.

SAMHSA National Helpline
1-800-662-4357 (HELP). Free, confidential, 24/7 information, support, and treatment referrals for mental health and substance-use concerns.

Disaster Distress Helpline
Call or text: 1-800-985-5990
24/7 crisis counselling for emotional distress related to natural or human-caused disasters.

CANADA
988 Suicide Crisis Helpline
Call or text: 988. Available 24 hours a day, 7 days a week for anyone in Canada experiencing suicidal thoughts, emotional distress, or concern about someone else.

Crisis Text Line Canada
Text HOME to 686868. Free, confidential crisis support by text.

item.title: I Love You Because You’re Different From Me
item.description:
Relationships

I Love You Because You’re Different From Me

Witnessing our differences may be the deepest form of loving connection.

Posted September 30, 2026

Key points
  • Difference in relationships does not have to mean disconnection.
  • Being witnessed is different than being agreed with or submitted to.
  • Love and connection deepen when we develop our capacity to witness differences.
Illustrated by Quiel Ramos
Source: Quiel Ramos: Illustrator

“Where are you?”

We all ask some version of this question when we experience a significant relational shift.

After years as a psychotherapist—with individuals, couples, and families—as well as decades of marriage, eight years as a parent, and living for half a century, I find that this utterly human question remains universal.

As the new school year approached, this question was very present for my son and his closest friends.

On the surface, of course, they asked one another: “What teacher did you get?” But what they meant was, “Where are you? Are we still together?”

And, when they discovered they were all assigned to different classrooms, they asked, “Where did you go?”

It's natural for kids who have formed deep friendships over time to wonder, nervously, whether their most familiar people will remain beside them as they enter a new school year.

September always brings an awareness of loss and change for all of us—new projects, new routines, less contact with the people, places, and things we’ve become attached to.

For my son and his friends, however, the changes this year were more palpable. It wasn’t just being in different classes, but they were also moving to a new building, and perhaps most significantly, they’d begun pursuing different interests. (Not all of them played baseball, or basketball, or tennis. Not all of them continued breakdancing. They would no longer spend every afternoon together, as they had come to expect.)

And yet, they remain deeply connected—not only in each other’s minds, but in their continuous recognition.

Talking with some of the parents, I found myself thinking about how much of our job—as parents, friends, family, and community—is learning to navigate connection, care, and love through witnessing difference.

The boys are discovering that being connected doesn’t require them to do everything together, every day. In fact, something novel, beautiful, and wonderfully alive happens when they don’t: They become more fully and freely themselves in the presence of one another.

Developmental research shows that autonomy and relatedness are not mutually exclusive needs, but can be cultivated together within intimate relationships, including friendships and eventually adult partnerships (Oudekerk, Allen, Hessel, and Mollow).

Developmental research on adolescents similarly suggests that autonomy and relatedness are not opposing needs, but can develop together within close friendships and later a range of adult relationships (Loeb and colleagues, 2021).

In this sense, differentiation in a relationship is not a threatening separation, but the necessary capacity to remain connected while inviting each participant to become more distinctly themselves. Research on couples similarly suggests that differentiation—the ability to maintain a coherent sense of self while remaining emotionally connected to people outside of us—is associated with healthy relational functioning. (Calatrava and colleagues, 2022).

So as much as we may all be driven by the absolute oneness that Plato illustrated in his origin of love story (and John Cameron Mitchell captured so unforgettably in his song The Origin of Love, from Hedwig and the Angry Inch), it seems to me that the deepest and most meaningful experience of love as a mortal human is much more profound than sameness.

I always tell couples I work with that it’s music to my ears whenever I hear one of them express unadulterated recognition of the other; even if they feel entirely alien to one another. I’m thinking now of a straight couple I worked with who were like oil and water. The husband began the first session by saying to me, “I guess you and my wife both see me as the ‘bad guy.’ Not sure why I even bothered showing up.”

His wife had spent years trying to help him understand the invisible load she carried as a co-parent of their two young sons. But whenever she asked for help or appreciation, he experienced her request as criticism. Every bid for recognition sounded to him like blame.

Rather than accepting their demand to cast me as Judge Judy, and to determine, unequivocally, who was right and who was wrong, I invited them to transcend the binary roles they had come to expect from one another.

“I’m not interested in who’s good or bad,” I told them. “I’m interested in whether the two of you can recognize each other’s true feelings and perspectives—beyond either of your expectations for how you ‘should’ be.”

For months, they practiced slowing down and reflecting on how their differences affected one another. Before responding defensively, each partner would breathe and reflect what they heard. The goal wasn’t submission to the other perspective, or agreement. It was simple, neutral recognition.

One afternoon, the husband turned to his wife and said: “Okay. I hear you saying you feel alone, that you’re carrying all the responsibility for our kids’ well-being. And that you need me to notice what needs to get done, rather than waiting for you to ask me every time. Is that right?”

His wife burst into tears. (And my eyes watered up, too). Nothing had been solved. But a pivotal event took place. His wife had been witnessed, truly seen and heard.

Witnessing that moment felt to me like hearing music—as it always does when people genuinely recognize one another, especially when they are very different.

Research on intimacy similarly points to the importance of what psychologists call perceived partner responsiveness: the experience that another person at least holds us in mind—if not understands, validates, and cares about us. Perceived responsiveness is considered a fundamental process in the development and maintenance of intimacy (Arican-Dinc and Gable, 2023).

I think this is what we are really asking for when we ask, “Where are you?”

Not necessarily: “Will you be exactly where I am, forever?”

Back to Plato. We are born into the world dreaming of a return to ultimate oneness. And then, we spend the rest of our lives negotiating the beautiful, and painful, reality that we cannot.

We may have flickers of that oneness—in an embrace, in sex, laughter, music, feeling understood.

But then we return to ourselves.

This is not a failure to love. This is what makes love possible as a mortal human being. Witnessing and being witnessed as separate and different.

Rather than anxiously asking “Where are you?” until we receive a momentary salve, we can instead take a moment to breathe, to see and hear one another, and to say: “There you are.”

item.title: Why We Are No Wiser Than Our Ancestors
item.description:
Wisdom

Why We Are No Wiser Than Our Ancestors

We know more and more—but understand less and less.

Posted September 30, 2026

Key points
  • Wisdom is not knowledge but perspective: seeing causes, connections, consequences, and limits.
  • Modern life gives us more information but less opportunity to understand what it means.
  • Wisdom requires the courage to see difficult truths, especially about ourselves.
Caspar David Friedrich’s Wanderer above the Sea of Fog (c. 1818). Greater perspective is the beginning of wisdom.
Source: Wikimedia Commons/Caspar David Friedrich/Public domain

Wisdom begins with the willingness to hear difficult truths, especially about ourselves. Our problem is not merely that we are no wiser than our ancestors; in many ways, we are less wise.

One reason for this is that we have abandoned wisdom as an ideal. The word "wisdom" appears 222 times in the Old Testament, and "philosophy" in the original Greek literally means "the love of wisdom." But today, anyone who speaks seriously about wisdom risks sounding grandiose or ridiculous—like me right now.

We admire intelligence, productivity, and innovation because they can be measured and monetised. Wisdom, however, is quieter, and often goes against the grain.

What Wisdom Is

Having replaced wisdom with expertise, we confuse knowing more with being wiser. But if wisdom simply amounted to knowledge, learning the name of every river and mountain in the world would make us wise, and every modern school-leaver would be wiser than a Socrates or a Seneca. Socrates was declared the wisest of men not because he knew everything, but because he understood what he did not know.

Aristotle took a different view. He said that wisdom is the understanding of causes: The wise person knows not merely that something is, but why it is. Wisdom consists in seeing the relations between things, for example, the immediate action and its distant consequences, or the present moment and the shape of an entire life. It’s not so much a kind of knowledge but a way of seeing, or ways of seeing.

Why We Lack Wisdom

If wisdom is perspective, our lack of wisdom becomes easier to explain. Today, knowledge is increasingly specialized and compartmentalized. Nobody is responsible for assembling the fragments or asking what they are for. There is no job description for someone like me, who falls between the cracks—and, unfortunately, no salary either.

In addition, we suffer from an overload of information. We’re always checking our phones, flitting from fragment to fragment, and living in abstract bubbles. Our ancestors may have known far less, but they were exposed to the rain and the wind: to nature, mortality, connection… to the things that can give us perspective.

Although, to be fair, our ancestors too struggled with wisdom. Wisdom derives from the Indo-European root, weid-, "to see." In Norse mythology, Odin sacrifices one eye at Mimir’s well in exchange for a higher kind of vision. Later, he hangs for nine nights from the world tree, pierced by his own spear, to win the runes. That’s what wisdom demands: the courage to see what we would rather not see.

item.title: The Art of Making Big Decisions: 7 Tips
item.description:
Decision-Making

The Art of Making Big Decisions: 7 Tips

Balancing emotional reactions with rational thinking in critical decisions.

Posted September 30, 2026

Key points
  • Major decisions can be overwhelming, causing anxiety about the future.
  • The keys are listening to your gut, being clear about your priorities, and being proactive.
  • It's also important to have support and to learn the lessons that the problems are teaching you.
Source: TheDigitalArtist/pixabay

Jake admits he’s frustrated with his current job and has been offered a new, more challenging role; he needs to decide within two weeks. Allyse has felt for a couple of years that her marriage has reached its end, but she’s understandably worried about the impact on the kids and what her future will look like.

Big decisions—about jobs, relationships, medical issues, or caring for family members—carry big emotional weight as you sort through options and hope you’ve made the right choice. Here are seven tips to help you navigate this challenge:

1. Go with your gut

Take the job or stay; leave the marriage or don’t? Your gut reaction is a good starting point and a counterpoint to all the pro-and-con junk likely swirling in your head.

That said, if you tend to be emotionally driven—doing what you do based on how you feel—or if you have ADHD, which makes you impulsive, it’s probably not a good idea to rely on your gut as your frontline decision-maker. Instead, slow down, step back, and bring your rational brain online and into the mix.

2. Be clear about what needs to be fixed

If Jake were to deconstruct his job frustration and Allyse her sense that the relationship has run its course, what, in ten words or less, is the problem? They need to know so the other affected person can know. If Jake’s supervisor or Allyse’s husband can’t articulate what Jake or Allyse are concretely looking for, and they only hear vague complaints or experience emotional outbursts, there is little opportunity for productive problem-solving.

But beyond problem-solving, the ability of Jake and Allyse to clearly define their problems is also tied to their ability to set priorities, recognize what’s missing from their lives, and decide what they want to move toward (not just escape from). This will allow Jake to emphasize what he needs most in his next job interview, and Allyse to know what to fight for during the divorce negotiations.

3. Decide at what point you’ve done your best

Jake has worked his way up the chain of command at his company and has been clear about what is needed. After months of couples therapy with little change, Allyse feels she has given it her best shot. Both are clear that they've done all they can in their current situation, and they are ready for a change. This is about understanding bottom lines and knowing when enough is enough.

4. Be clear about your concerns as you look ahead

If Jake knows he wants to take the new job but is worried about the learning curve, or if Allyse knows she wants to leave but is concerned about how the children will cope, acknowledging their concerns rather than sweeping them under the rug can help them be proactive and develop a plan to ease their worries. Jake can talk with his new supervisor about expectations and training; Allyse can explore support options through the children’s schools or request referrals to child therapists.

5. Imagine the worst-case scenario

This is also about being proactive and planning. If Jake doesn’t get the new job because the company has decided to freeze hiring, or if Allyse feels that leaving will be too disastrous for her children, brainstorming what they can do and what they need to cope helps prevent them from feeling trapped and victimized. Jake may decide to bring in a headhunter, or Allyse may rely more on friends and family to help her get more of what is missing in the marriage.

6. Know the moral of the story

As is always the case, there are take-away lessons for Jake and Allyse about their job and marriage, a moral to the story they can carry forward regardless of what decision they make. For instance, perhaps Jake needed to be more assertive, or Allyse ignored red flags far too long.

But they need to be careful that the moral they come away with isn’t too simple or reductionistic—Jake blames his supervisor for micromanaging, or Allyse blames her husband for drinking too much. These one-liners don’t help them understand the relationship dynamics; they leave out their own role in the story, which can be important information as they move forward.

7. Reach out to others

Finally, while making big decisions requires you to be deliberate and proactive, and ultimately the final decision is yours alone, don’t hesitate to reach out to others for support—to serve as a sounding board for your thoughts, to play devil’s advocate, or simply to affirm what you’re thinking and saying. Don’t make the process a solo act.

And don’t be surprised if your perspective shifts over time

If Jake is happy with his new job two years from now, he will be glad he left, or even kick himself for not leaving sooner; ditto for Allyse, if she gets divorced. But if Jake is miserable or Allyse’s kids are struggling, Jake may feel he was too impulsive, or Allyse may wish she had tried a little longer.

We’re always filtering our past through the lens of the present, creating an ever-changing perspective, with our feelings being a moving target.

As always, simply do the best you can.

item.title: BTS: The Science of Choosing to Be Present
item.description:
Social Life

BTS: The Science of Choosing to Be Present

What happens in the brain when you stop documenting and start experiencing.

Posted September 30, 2026

Key points
  • Most people film concerts they rarely rewatch and enjoy less for having done it.
  • Being physically present with others produces more emotion.
  • An invitation to presence works differently from a ban on phones.
What happens when thousands of people choose to put their phones down at the same time?
Source: Laura Bilbao Broch / Used with permission

I need the whole stadium to jump, put your phone down, let’s get all the fun. — From “Body to Body” by BTS

At the start of their current world tour, BTS open with a song called “Body to Body” and a simple instruction: Put your phone down.

And fifty to ninety thousand people do.

Nobody is forced to. There are no pouches being snapped over their phones at the entrance, no staff confiscating devices, no threat of being thrown out. Someone simply asks, and the request is obeyed.

I was there in Brussels, watching it happen, and I found myself thinking about how amazing that moment was.

The research tells us that we already know what filming a concert can cost us. A Heineken study of Gen Z and Millennial concert-goers found that 55% admitted they prioritised filming over being present. Yet 60% said they would enjoy concerts more if they disconnected, while 13% rarely went back to watch the footage they had spent the evening capturing.

We know filming can get in the way of the experience but we do it anyway, at least until someone reminds us that we don't have to.

A randomised controlled study published earlier this year in Scientific Reports compared 130 participants watching either a live concert or a simultaneous cinematic livestream of the same event (Becker et al., 2026).

The people who attended in person reported greater appreciation for the music, greater emotional arousal and higher levels of kama muta—the feeling of being moved, often accompanied by warmth, chills or a sense of connection.

The music and the songs were the same. What changed was being physically there with other people.

Another study, published in Computers in Human Behavior Reports in 2024, points towards one possible explanation. Kulla and colleagues found that social presence, the feeling that other people are genuinely there with you, mediated the relationship between the concert experience and wellbeing (Kulla et al., 2024). Part of what makes a collective experience different is knowing that thousands of other people are experiencing it alongside you.

When thousands of people put their phones down at once, they suddenly become a room.

Why an Invitation Works Better Than a Ban

Some performers and venues have tried to solve the phone problem by taking choice away altogether mandating that devices be locked into pouches and designating specific phone-use areas. The evidence on these approaches is mixed, as audiences do not always respond enthusiastically to having their choices restricted.

There is a psychological reason that may explain why. Reactance is the tendency to resist when we feel that our freedom to choose has been threatened. Take an option away and, perversely, that option can become more appealing.

Which makes the wording of the BTS approach interesting: Put your phone down is not the same psychological message as you cannot use your phone. One is a restriction, while the other is an invitation. That distinction does not eliminate reactance, and we cannot know from one concert alone exactly why people complied. But it changes the framing, as the audience retains the choice.

Remember those Heineken numbers: More than half of the people surveyed said they prioritised filming over being present, while 60% said they would enjoy concerts more if they disconnected. That sounds less like a population that desperately wants to film everything and more like one caught between two competing desires: We want the footage but we also want the experience.

Why are we filming in the first place? It is easy to assume that people are doing it for social media, and sometimes they are, but research on concert photography suggests the motivation can be much more sympathetic: People want to preserve an experience that feels important and temporary. The phone becomes a kind of prosthetic memory—a guarantee that this really happened.

I understand that impulse. You are standing in a stadium watching something you have waited months or years to see, and some part of your brain is already aware that the moment is disappearing while you are experiencing it, but that recording also changes what you are doing.

You may start watching the performance through a six-inch rectangle even though the person you came to see is standing in front of you and so the attempt to preserve the experience can start competing with the experience itself. That's what makes the BTS moment so interesting to me. They were not really asking people to give up their memories; just to stop trying to manufacture a record of the moment while they were still inside it.

What Happens When Everyone Chooses the Same Thing?

Hopkins and colleagues (2015) found that positive emotional experiences during large collective events were associated with the extent to which people felt able to express their social identity as part of the group and experienced a sense of connection with those around them. That makes intuitive sense; there is something psychologically different about standing among thousands of strangers and realising that, for three hours, you are all here for the same reason.

The person next to you may not know your name, but you do not need to have anything else in common because you are both screaming the same lyrics. You both know what is about to happen. And you both react when the lights go down.

When everyone around you makes the same decision to put their phones away, the decision itself becomes part of the experience.

A stadium full of people filming the same stage is still a collection of individuals, but a stadium full of people who have collectively decided to stop filming for a moment becomes something else.

That moment in Brussels wasn't really about phones but permission.

We live with a strange kind of background pressure to document our lives, and underneath that is another pressure: Keep one eye on what might be happening somewhere else. Maybe there is a better angle, or something interesting is happening in the crowd, or maybe someone is posting something you should see. You should be documenting this properly because, otherwise, what will you have left? The result: Even when we are somewhere extraordinary, part of our attention can remain slightly outside the room.

BTS reminded people that there was another choice available.

The desire to record a concert and the desire to experience it fully are not opposites. The phone is there because we care about what is happening enough to want to keep it. The problem is that sometimes the attempt to preserve an experience gets in the way of having it.

item.title: How to Use Tips Based on Neuroscience to Relieve Stress
item.description:
Neuroscience

How to Use Tips Based on Neuroscience to Relieve Stress

It can take less than 15 minutes to stop worrying and become happier.

Posted September 30, 2026

Key points
  • Advances in neuroscience have enabled us to understand how to rebalance our nervous system quickly.
  • Ancient spiritual practices, like meditation and body scans, have been proven useful for psychological issues.
  • These tips are easy to learn and can often diminish stress and elevate our mood in under 15 minutes.
  • The methods in this post are quite discrete and can usually be done without anyone else noticing.
Source: Elinor Greenberg/AI-Generated Image, ChatGPT

Life can feel hard at times, and most of us want a break from stress. But we do not necessarily have the time or opportunity to do one of the tried and true methods, such as taking a vacation, going for a walk in nature, or socializing with friends.

The good news is that advances in neuroscience over the last 20 years have helped psychologists identify simple, low cost ways to lift our mood that take under 15 minutes. These all use what we have learned about our brain and body/mind system to directly and quickly rebalance us wherever we are, whenever we want.

These tools can be used with psychotherapy or on your own.

I teach these methods to my clients as self-care tools. One that I included below was just invented by a creative client to support herself between therapy sessions. I have permission to share it.

I enjoy finding ways that make happiness easier to achieve. To that end, I have been collecting tips that quickly, and somewhat effortlessly, shift our mind away from our worries and lift our mood. You can think of these activities as easy, affordable, mini-vacations that can quickly reset your mind/body system.

Nature Viewing

We know from neuroscience research that most humans find being out in nature calming (Bratman et al., 2015). But did you know that just looking at appealing pictures of nature can help reset your mood and restore your previously depleted ability to focus (Ulrich et al., 1991)?

Try it for yourself. Choose some pretty nature images and load them on your phone and computer. Or, keep a favorite framed on your desk. When you need a lift or want to feel refreshed, look at your chosen image closely for 20 seconds.

Notice your favorite parts of the picture and how focusing on what you find visually appealing, such as a sunset, bird, or waterfall, can interrupt unpleasant thoughts and be pleasantly absorbing.

Check If You Are Breathing

I know this sounds strange, but it actually works. If you want to quickly stop thinking of something unpleasant, check if you are breathing. Something about switching your attention to your body, and evaluating something concrete like breathing vs. not breathing, shifts your brain from the hypothetical (worrying) to an entirely different track (Farb et al, 2023).

Look Outward, Not Inward

It is actually our choice whether we look inward at ourself or outward at other people. Our brain and sensory organs have their limits. You cannot easily look inward and outward at the same time.

So if you are feeling self-conscious in a social situation, simply switch your attention from inward, where you are evaluating yourself, to outward, and engage the other person instead. This is not about searching for their flaws. It is about looking at the other person and concentrating on them instead of yourself.

One of the benefits of this method is that you might learn something useful about this person and your relationship. And most people appreciate getting their companion’s complete attention.

Here are some potentially useful things you can pay attention to:

Tone: Do I like their tone of voice?

Focus: What topics does this person bring up or like to talk about?

Attitude: If I were describing their attitude to someone else after this conversation, how would I describe it? Is it pleasant, neutral, enthusiastic, bored, or hostile?

As you can see, the basic principle is simple. If you have a tendency to be judgmental, you just switch direction and use that tool on the other person instead of yourself. Your tendency to be judgmental can be put to better use than beating yourself up again for your flaws.

Be a Pretend Host

This tool uses reframing your situation to shift your mood. Instead of thinking like a guest, think like a host. As with the prior tip, this involves shifting from focusing on yourself to focusing on other people.

You are not the only person who feels nervous and self-conscious at parties.

Instead of focusing on how you feel, focus on the other guests instead. Imagine it is your job as a self-appointed host or hostess to notice guests who appear lonely or uncomfortable. When you find one, go up and start a light conversation. You are likely to feel better helping someone else than worrying about the impression you are making.

10 Minute Body Scan

We have lots of good research that shows that brief body scans reduce stress very effectively for most people.

What is a body scan?

Many of us are too busy thinking, working, or doing chores to pay much attention to what our body is experiencing. Modern life tends to be fast paced and require a lot of cognitive activity. Outside of normal self-care, like brushing our teeth, most of us only pay attention to our body if we are exercising, pursuing sensual enjoyment, or are in pain.

A body scan is a type of mindfulness meditation that starts at the top of your head and gradually works its way down your body. Some versions start at your feet and work up.

Step 1–Take 3 deep, slow, breaths to start relaxing.

Step 2–Do your best to have no assumptions.

Instead of assuming you know what you are feeling, keep a very open mind. Most people are a bit surprised at what they find. Sometimes we expect an area to hurt and it does not. Other times we discover areas of tension that we can relax and release.

Step 3–Return if you drift.

As with other types of meditation, if your attention shifts and you find yourself thinking about something else, just gently return to focusing on your body (Sparacio, A., et al., 2024)

Set Your Timer

My client invented this one. If you know that your mind often drifts into pointless worrying or self-reproach, you might want to try this tip as an experiment.

Step 1–Set your timer.

Set your phone timer to go off every 15 minutes.

Step 2–Check your thoughts.

When it rings, check what you are thinking. If you fell down some unpleasant rabbit hole, you can reset your thinking back to something more neutral or comforting using one of the above methods.

Summary

We used to have to guess at what might cheer us up. And often what worked was fun but also expensive and time consuming. Modern neuroscience has given us the knowledge that our brain is more easily changed than we once believed. It turns out that there are lots of shortcuts that directly target our mind/body system that can help us feel calmer and happier without a lot of extra work.

item.title: Dog Trainers Switch Methods Due to Empathy and Education
item.description:
Animal Behavior

Dog Trainers Switch Methods Due to Empathy and Education

Dog trainers' approaches are motivated by differing beliefs on ethics and science.

Posted September 30, 2026

Key points
  • Reward-based methods are better for dogs and the human-animal bond, but some trainers still use aversives.
  • A study found that reward-based trainers put emphasis on education while aversives trainers value experience.
  • Trainers who switched to a modern approach say it was because of empathy for dogs and better education.

The scientific evidence on dog training methods shows that the use of aversives (such as prong and shock collars or tugs on the leash) has risks for dog welfare and for the dog-human relationship. But dog training is not regulated, and some trainers still use these outdated methods.

New research published in Frontiers in Veterinary Science sheds light on the differing viewpoints of American reward-based and aversive trainers. The results show that while both types of dog trainer say they take good dog welfare into account, reward-based trainers put much more emphasis on a formal education. Perhaps unsurprisingly, aversive trainers put more emphasis on their experience, and claim—despite the evidence of the risks, the position statements from veterinary and animal welfare organizations, and the abilities of their reward-based colleagues—that sometimes they need to use aversive methods.

Jamie DeLeeuw, Ph.D., of Community Research Plus and first author of the study, told me in an email,

“What we would most want ordinary dog guardians to take away is that training is not just about stopping behavior—it is about understanding what dogs are communicating and supporting the relationship they have with the people who care for them.

“One of the most heartening things we found was that, even in a polarized field, the certification-affiliated trainers we interviewed shared important common ground around canine welfare, owner education, and the value of positive reinforcement. At the same time, owners are often trying to make decisions in a confusing and largely unregulated field, where trainers may make very different claims about what is humane or effective.

“For dog guardians, I think the key is to be wary of quick fixes and to look for a trainer who can clearly explain their approach, prioritize the dog’s emotional and physical well-being, and help them understand the emotions and needs behind the behavior. Behaviors that look like “defiance” are often rooted in fear, frustration, anxiety, confusion, or a mismatch between the dog’s needs and environment. A good trainer should help both the dog and the guardian learn—not simply suppress behavior.”

How Was the Study Done?

The study involved detailed interviews with 35 dog trainers in the U.S. The trainers were found via the directories of the International Association of Animal Behavior Consultants (IAABC), the Certification Council for Professional Dog Trainers (CCPDT), and the International Association of Canine Professionals (IACP). At the time of data collection, IAABC and CCPDT followed a joint ethical approach called LIMA (Least Invasive, Minimally Aversive) that prioritizes positive reinforcement but allows for the use of aversives. (It’s worth noting that the IAABC subsequently updated its position and now its members must use reward-based methods). The IACP’s position statement on dog training methods cites LIMA as justifying the use of aversives.

Source: New Africa/Shutterstock

While it may be confusing that all three organizations either support or supported LIMA, the dog trainers in the study could be easily divided into two camps: those who sometimes use aversive methods (some might call them “balanced” trainers), and those who never do (reward-based trainers). Interestingly, the group of trainers who never use aversive methods were selected because they had used them in the past; in other words they are “crossover” trainers who have switched to reward-based methods. All of the trainers completed a short survey and then took part in an interview that asked about their perspectives on dog training. The transcripts were analyzed to identify the most important themes.

What Do the Results Tell Us?

Dog training is a divided industry, but both the aversive and reward-based trainers raised concerns about lack of regulation. The trainers who used aversives said that they mostly used positive reinforcement, and only sometimes felt they needed to use aversives. Both groups of trainers expressed concerns about dog guardians having unrealistic expectations and not understanding canine body language or what dogs need.

Trainers in both groups said they were concerned about dogs’ emotional well-being, but there were differences in whether they felt it was okay for dogs to be stressed in training, and on the effectiveness and ethics of using aversive methods. Reward-based trainers gave much more positive ratings for the effectiveness of classical conditioning (often used to help fearful dogs), and much lower ratings for the effectiveness of positive punishment (used by aversive trainers to suppress behavior) than the aversive trainers did.

One interesting finding is on views about education, where trainers who use aversives are prioritizing experience over education. The success of their colleagues who have crossed over to become reward-based trainers shows the value of a formal education in dog training. While the aversive trainers said they had moved on from dominance approaches to training, they also disputed much of the scientific research on training methods.

Meanwhile, the crossover trainers said their switch to reward-based methods came about as they developed more empathic feelings towards dogs and had more exposure to the use of positive reinforcement. For some it was a gradual change, while others had a specific “aha” moment that led them to stop using aversives.

Discussions about the importance of education have occurred in many different fields over the years as part of moves towards professionalization. There are some interesting comparisons with an earlier study in Canada (Cavalli & Fenwick, 2025), which found that most Canadian dog trainers use reward-based methods, but that around a third are self-taught and many share concerns about lack of regulation.

The lack of regulation in the dog training industry makes it confusing for dog guardians. If you’re looking for a dog trainer, check that they will use reward-based methods to train your dog; membership of an organization such as the Pet Professional Guild, International Association of Animal Behaviour Consultants, the Association of Professional Dog Trainers, or the Canadian Association of Professional Dog Trainers is one thing to look for. As well, the American Veterinary Society for Animal Behaviour has a helpful position statement on how to choose a dog trainer that lists red and green flags.

item.title: The Price of Pride
item.description:
Forgiveness

The Price of Pride

The hidden costs of refusing to apologize.

Posted September 30, 2026

Key points
  • Holding onto guilt can be harmful, both mentally and physically.
  • When we apologize for our mistakes, we drastically reduce our guilt.
  • Practice makes perfect! You can learn to get better at saying sorry.
The price of pride can sometimes be isolation.
Source: Tim Marshall/StockSnap

You’ve just said something insensitive and hurtful to someone you care about. They are angry, and you feel terrible. You know you should say sorry, but you also worry that admitting you made a mistake could make you look weak. You remain silent, choosing your pride over the relationship.

It’s easy to imagine ourselves in this situation. Making a genuine, sincere apology is hard. Admitting to having acted badly comes with risks: that the apology won’t be accepted, that they might think worse of us, that other people will judge us. But research shows that while apologizing can be difficult, not apologizing can be even harder. Keeping our guilt to ourselves can take a heavy toll on us, both mentally and physically.


Psychological Effects of Unaddressed Guilt

The psychological costs of carrying unaddressed guilt can lead to what's known as "moral distress" - feelings of anxiety, sadness, and even depression (VanderWeele et al., 2025). It’s what we feel when our actions don’t align with our core beliefs. You likely view yourself as a good, empathetic person, but the fact that you just hurt someone creates cognitive dissonance: only “bad” people hurt others, right?

This isn’t true, of course - we all make mistakes - but since we naturally tend to tie our self-worth to being “good,” admitting fault feels like a threat to our identity. Apologizing can resolve that dissonance, because it sends a signal, both to us and to the person we hurt, that we know we made a mistake and feel bad about it. This helps the person we hurt forgive us, and it also helps us forgive ourselves. This matters because, ultimately, human connection is essential to our mental health. When we don’t apologize, it can damage these relationships, making us feel isolated and lonely.

Withholding an apology can also affect us physically. A 2023 study by Chloe Stewart and colleagues mapped the physical effects of guilt in healthy adults. When they compared the physiological responses of those who reported feeling neutral to those who reported experiencing guilt after watching a video clip, they found that guilt has a particular “autonomic signature.” Compared to a neutral state, guilt was associated with increased swallowing and lower gastric activity, which accounts for the sinking feeling we have when we realize we’ve done something wrong. In the short-term, these feelings aren’t physically harmful, but if you continue to feel guilty about what you did, your body stays in a state of stress that can eventually take a toll on your health.

How to Practice and Improve Apologizing

The good news is that apologizing is a skill you can practice and improve. Here are three ways to start:

1. “Micro-dose” your apologies

Think of apologizing as a muscle that you need to build up. Choose something small and relatively minor to start with; you don’t need to reopen a longstanding family feud at this point. The next time you accidentally bump into someone, or are five minutes late, or forget to return a text or phone call, own up to it right away. Trying saying, “I’m sorry; that was my fault.” Notice how you feel afterwards. Was it as hard as you thought it would be? Notice how warmly the other person responds.

2. Ask the difficult question

The next time you feel hesitant to apologize, stop and ask yourself: Would I rather protect my pride, or protect my relationship with this person? Relationships are vital to our wellbeing. Your desire to protect your ego might be getting in the way of having a meaningful connection with this person.

3. Don’t overcomplicate it

A good apology doesn’t need to be an elaborate performance. It only needs to do two basic things: show that you feel remorse and validate the feelings of the person you hurt. You can do this by making sure that in your apology you:

  • Take responsibility for what you did
  • Say (or show) that you are sorry
  • Make amends, if you can
  • Indicate that you will do your best to ensure that it doesn’t happen again

Above all, remember that apologizing isn’t a sign of weakness. As I explore in my upcoming book, Say It Like You Mean It, a genuine apology can be one of the most powerful things we do to repair relationships and bring people back together. People who are willing to admit to their mistakes and apologize for them are seen as more trustworthy, emotionally mature, and competent (Fetterman et al., 2022; Rutjens et al., 2023). Being able to show true remorse signals to others that you have a secure sense of who you are and can handle seeing yourself as imperfect.

Refusing to apologize is a lonely place. You may be protecting your ego, but it can come at the cost of true connection.

item.title: When Quiet in a Marriage Isn’t Peace
item.description:
Marriage

When Quiet in a Marriage Isn’t Peace

A quieter marriage may reflect resignation, not genuine peace or acceptance.

Posted September 30, 2026

Key points
  • When one partner stops trying, less conflict can mask a deeper loss of intimacy and connection.
  • Resignation is not acceptance; it often means someone has stopped believing their needs will be met.
  • A quieter marriage isn't always healthier. Get curious about whether the silence reflects peace or giving up.
Disengaged couple
Source: Andrik Langfield / Unsplash

We often call marriage a partnership, and that implies equality, sharing the load, or divvying up tasks and responsibilities in a way that feels fair. Sometimes that means one person does more than the other because they have more capacity. That can also include more relational tending – planning dates, trips, nurturing the other and the relationship emotionally, or reading books. However, in my practice as a psychologist and sex therapist, what I witness frequently is a relationship that has become profoundly unequal.

Rather than two people actively working on the marriage, there’s only one. There's only one person who leans into intimacy, suggests therapy, reads books, listens to podcasts, schedules dates, and does all the things that are recommended for a good and healthy marriage to flourish. They are doing their part but their spouse?...Their supposed partner?...Not so much.

The participatory partner may keep trying for a while…sometimes a long while. They may keep making bids for connection, but those bids are not met. There can be years of little moments where they reach toward their spouse, and the spouse does not reach back. It hurts and it adds up. Eventually, the participatory partner lessens the bids more and more and then stops. They stop sending articles or podcasts to their spouse. They stop asking for dates. They stop bringing up their relationship needs. They stop initiating affection that isn't reciprocated. They often are still pursued for sexual connection by their spouse, though, which can be confusing. “Why are they pursuing me for sex but not for emotional intimacy?” the thinking goes.

The participatory partner stops trying to explain what they need because they've already explained it so many times, and it still goes unmet. They just give up. Not dramatically, often quietly. They “quiet quit” their marriage. The couple is still legally married; they still handle parenting and the logistics of life, but no one is participating anymore – not with presence, not with attention, and not with care. The structure of the marriage or relationship has remained intact even as its vitality has slowly drained away.

Something important happens when the participatory partner quietly quits the marriage. The other partner can think the marriage is actually better because there’s less fighting and complaining. There are fewer demands. Nobody is asking them to read something or go to therapy or have another conversation. They might experience this as peace.

The formerly participatory partner may continue in this vein for years — not expecting much, not getting much, just coasting. But they may also decide to end the marriage eventually, and this is where things get interesting. In my experience working with couples, the other partner can be completely shocked. And I mean genuinely shocked, and even confused, and possibly devastated, and deeply hurt. They may have experienced the quieter marriage as evidence that things had actually improved, so the decision to leave may seem like it came out of nowhere.

There are two different realities at play. The formerly participatory partner felt the marriage ending little by little over time, whereas the other partner experiences the loss when their spouse says, “I’m leaving.” The formerly participatory partner may think, “How can you be surprised? I’ve been telling you for years I’m unhappy.” But for the other partner, they may think, “You stopped complaining. I just assumed it didn’t bother you anymore and that you accepted this is who I am and how I behave.”

Acceptance may imply peace; but it’s not the same thing as “giving up.” My patients may accept things like, “My spouse is an early riser,” but that’s not the same thing as resignation. Resignation is closer to defeat: “I’ll never get what I want so I’m going to stop asking.” There’s an inherent disappointment and grief in resignation that doesn’t exist with acceptance.

I’m not suggesting that if your partner goes quiet you’re automatically headed for a divorce. I can’t possibly predict that. But it’s something to pay attention to when the quiet begins to expand across the relationship. It’s one thing if your spouse stops complaining that you leave the toilet seat up. It’s another if they stop talking about all the things that once really mattered to them. Rather than mind-reading, get curious about what the quiet actually means. Did something get resolved? Did someone arrive at genuine acceptance? Or did they stop believing that reaching toward you would make any difference?

Perhaps what deserves your attention isn’t whether a marriage has become quieter, but how it became quiet.
